overview.title: 📖 Overview: Nullification in a Majority, From Blood to Brine
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 22a–22b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves the open question from the end of 21b: the mass of congealed blood must be buried simply to publicize that the mother is now exempt from a future firstborn — implying it really is a full-fledged offspring. Rabbi Yoḥanan then explains why it still doesn't impart ritual impurity: it is nullified within the majority of the surrounding mass, the same principle he finds underlying a parallel ruling of Rabbi Shimon about a disintegrated fetus in an afterbirth. A technical digression defines the precise size — a 'skein' (פִּיקָּה) of thread — at which a fetus's head begins to impart impurity, differing between a woman and an animal. The Gemara then pivots to a wider exploration of nullification in a majority through the case of purchasing fish brine from an unreliable seller, and finally through the dispute over whether a se'a of impure teruma that fell into non-sacred produce can ever have its impurity 'revive.'

slides.title: 🩸 Why Bury Something That Isn't Impure?
slides.subtitle: Resolving the question left open at the end of 21b

nodes.content: ❓ The mass of congealed blood must be buried, yet doesn't impart impurity by touch or carrying — so is it a real offspring or not?
⚖️ Answer: it is buried simply to publicize that the mother is exempt from a future firstborn — meaning it IS a full-fledged offspring
🔍 So why doesn't it impart impurity like a real fetus should?
✅ Rabbi Yoḥanan: it is nullified within the majority of the surrounding congealed mass — the Sages 'touched upon' it only enough to exclude it from tumah by contact or carrying

callout.label: Key concept:
callout.text: בִּיטּוּל בְּרוֹב — a minority substance loses its independent halakhic identity when submerged within a larger majority.

slides.title: 🧶 How Big Must a Fetus's Head Be to Impart Impurity?
slides.subtitle: The skein (פִּיקָּה) measures — three tannaitic opinions, then a final ruling
rows: A skein of woof threads (עֵרֶב) — coarser and thicker
From when tefifiyot appear — folds like those seen when a mule crouches to urinate
A woman's fetus: the finer warp-thread skein; an animal's fetus: the coarser woof-thread skein
The larger sack-makers' skein — used to measure a clod of earth from a doubtful gravesite, not fetal size

callout.label: Transmission chain:
callout.text: Rav Huna knew of two skeins but couldn't identify them; Rav Dimi added a third in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name; only when Ravin arrived was the ruling finally clarified.

slides.title: 👥 Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon 'Said the Same Thing'
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan finds one underlying principle behind two very different rulings

boxes.title: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items: A mass of congealed blood from a large animal is a real offspring — hence buried, and the mother is exempt from a future firstborn
Yet it does not impart impurity, since it is nullified within the majority of the mass

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon
items: When a woman's afterbirth is found in a house, the house becomes impure — since there is no afterbirth without an offspring inside it
But if the fetus disintegrated before emerging, the house stays pure — the disintegrated fetus is nullified within the majority afterbirth

callout.label: Shared principle:
callout.text: In both cases, a real fetal presence is halakhically real, yet vanishes from legal significance once submerged in the majority of surrounding, non-fetal material.

slides.title: 🐟 Purifying Fish Brine From an Unreliable Seller
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, applies bittul berov

lines.speaker: R' Lakish
lines.text: One who buys brine from an am ha'aretz may bring it into contact with a ritual bath's water, and it becomes pure.

lines.speaker: Reasoning
lines.text: מִמָּה נַפְשָׁךְ — whichever way you look at it: if water is the majority, contact purifies it; if brine is the majority, brine itself can't contract impurity anyway, and the minority water is nullified within it.

lines.speaker: R' Yirmeya
lines.text: This works only for dipping bread. For cooking in a pot with other water, it does not — the once-nullified water 'finds its own kind' and revives its impurity.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Can nullified impurity really return and revive?

lines.speaker: Rav Dimi
lines.text: Yes — and there is a proof from the teruma mishna, about a se'a of impure teruma that fell into one hundred se'a of pure produce.

callout.label: Setting up the next question:
callout.text: This exchange launches the Gemara into the teruma dispute over whether nullified impurity can ever be reactivated.

slides.title: 🌾 Does Nullified Impurity Ever Revive?
slides.subtitle: A se'a of impure teruma falls into one hundred se'a of pure, non-sacred produce

steps.content: 1️⃣ Case: the impure teruma is now a tiny minority within a huge quantity of ordinary produce
2️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer: remove one se'a from the mixture and let it rot as impure teruma — 'the se'a that fell is the se'a that arose,' as if the impurity never truly vanished
3️⃣ The Rabbis: let the teruma be fully nullified — all 101 se'a become non-sacred and may be eaten
4️⃣ But even the Rabbis add a caution: keep the mixture away from water, since contact with water could make it susceptible to new impurity
5️⃣ Workarounds: eat it dry or roasted, knead it with fruit juice instead of water, or divide it into small batches so no single batch holds an egg-bulk of the original teruma

callout.label: Connection to Bekhorot 22:
callout.text: This debate over whether nullification is permanent or reversible is the same conceptual question raised by the mass of congealed blood and the fish brine — is bittul a true erasure, or just a temporary suppression?

summary.principle: Nullification in a majority (בִּיטּוּל בְּרוֹב) lets a real but minority presence — a fetus, a drop of water, a se'a of teruma — lose its independent legal force, though the Gemara debates whether that suppression is ever truly permanent.

flowSteps.content: 🩸 The buried mass of congealed blood is a real offspring, nullified within the majority so it doesn't impart impurity
🧶 A parallel technical measure: the skein-sized fetal head that finally triggers impurity, differing for woman and animal
👥 Rabbi Yoḥanan unites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon under the same nullification principle

columns.content: 🐟 Fish brine is pure 'whichever way you look at it' — but cooking can revive nullified impurity
🌾 Rabbi Eliezer vs. the Rabbis: does a nullified se'a of teruma ever truly disappear?

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: A minority substance's halakhic identity can be suppressed by a majority, but whether that suppression is permanent remains a live dispute

quiz.q: Why must the mass of congealed blood be buried, according to the Gemara's resolution at the start of the daf?
o: Because it definitely imparts ritual impurity
To publicize that the mother is now exempt from having a future offspring counted a firstborn
Because it is halakhically identical to an ordinary firstborn animal
Because burial is required for all animal remains
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that burial serves to publicize the mother's new exemption from firstborn status for future offspring — implying that the mass really is treated as a full-fledged offspring.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, why doesn't the mass of congealed blood impart ritual impurity through contact or carrying, if it is a real offspring?
o: Because congealed blood is never impure
Because it is nullified within the majority of the surrounding mass
Because only human fetuses impart this type of impurity
Because the mother's status protects it
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that although the offspring is real, it is nullified (בִּיטּוּל בְּרוֹב) within the larger congealed mass, so it does not impart impurity by touch or carrying.

quiz.q: What did Rabbi Yoḥanan mean when he said Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon 'said the same thing'?
o: They disagreed about everything except the definition of a firstborn
Both rulings rest on the principle that a real fetal presence is nullified when submerged within a majority of non-fetal material
Both rabbis discussed only human pregnancies
They both ruled that fetuses never impart impurity under any circumstances
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan connects Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling on the congealed mass to Rabbi Shimon's ruling on a disintegrated fetus in an afterbirth — both apply the same principle of nullification in a majority.

quiz.q: According to Reish Lakish, why is brine purchased from an unreliable seller (am ha'aretz) pure after contact with a ritual bath, regardless of the mixture's composition?
o: Brine can never become impure under any circumstances
If water is the majority, contact purifies it; if brine is the majority, brine itself cannot contract impurity and the minority water is nullified
The seller's unreliability is irrelevant to purity law
Ritual baths only purify solid objects, not liquids
quiz.e: Reish Lakish's 'מִמָּה נַפְשָׁךְ' argument covers both possibilities: whichever substance is the majority, the result is purity — either through direct purification of the water, or through nullification of the minority water within the brine.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Rabbi Eliezer's and the Rabbis' positions on a se'a of impure teruma that fell into one hundred se'a of pure, non-sacred produce?
o: Rabbi Eliezer says the whole mixture is permanently forbidden; the Rabbis say it is always fully permitted with no restrictions
Rabbi Eliezer says one se'a must be removed and left to rot as impure; the Rabbis say the teruma is nullified but caution against contact with water
There is no practical difference between their positions
Rabbi Eliezer permits eating the mixture freely, while the Rabbis forbid it entirely
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer holds that a se'a must be removed and treated as impure teruma, while the Rabbis hold the teruma is nullified and the whole mixture becomes non-sacred — though they still caution against exposing it to water, which could make it newly susceptible to impurity.
